title: 10 — Relational Databases
html:
10 — Relational Databases

Premise: the database is where most production performance problems and most data-correctness bugs live. Knowing SQL syntax is table stakes; knowing how the engine executes it is the senior skill.

1. How a query actually executes

flowchart LR
    A[SQL text] --> B[Parser<br/>syntax → tree]
    B --> C[Binder<br/>resolve names, types, permissions]
    C --> D[Optimiser<br/>enumerate plans, cost them<br/>using STATISTICS]
    D --> E[Plan cache]
    E --> F[Execution engine<br/>operators: scan, seek, join, sort, aggregate]
    F --> G[Storage engine<br/>buffer pool → pages → disk]
    G --> H[Transaction + lock manager<br/>+ WAL / transaction log]

The three facts this diagram encodes:

  1. The optimiser is cost-based and driven by statistics. Stale or missing statistics ⇒ wrong cardinality estimate ⇒ wrong plan (e.g. a nested-loop join over 5 million rows). Most "the query suddenly got slow" incidents are this.
  2. Everything is pages in a buffer pool. A query's cost is dominated by how many pages it must touch, and whether they're in memory. 8 KB pages in SQL Server and Postgres.
  3. Durability comes from the write-ahead log. COMMIT means "the log record is on stable storage", not "the data page is written". Data pages are flushed later by a checkpoint. This is why commits are fast and why the log disk is the one that must be fast.

2. Storage: B+ trees, heaps, and the LSM alternative

2.1 Table organisation

Heap Clustered index (index-organised table)
Row location Unordered pages Rows stored in the B+ tree leaves, ordered by the clustering key
Lookup by key Needs a nonclustered index → then a RID lookup Direct seek to the row
Range scan on the key Random I/O Sequential
Default Postgres tables are heaps + separate indexes SQL Server: PK is clustered by default; MySQL/InnoDB: always clustered on PK

Consequence in SQL Server / InnoDB: every nonclustered index leaf stores the clustering key as the row pointer. So a wide clustering key (e.g. a varchar(200) natural key) is duplicated into every index → bloat everywhere. Keep the clustering key narrow, unique, static, and ever-increasing.

⚠️ Random GUID primary keys (NEWID(), Guid.NewGuid()) as the clustered key cause: page splits throughout the tree, fragmentation, poor cache locality, and 4× the index size vs an int. Use int/bigint identity, NEWSEQUENTIALID(), UUIDv7, or ULID if you need a client-generated, non-enumerable, time-ordered key.

2.2 B+ tree cost model (recap from file 03 §5.3)

Height = log_fanout(rows). With ~400 keys per 8 KB page: 1M rows ≈ 3 levels, 1B rows ≈ 4–5 levels. The top levels are always cached. This is why an index seek is ~O(1) in practice regardless of table size, and why adding rows rarely slows a seek — but a scan grows linearly.

2.3 B-tree vs LSM tree

B+ tree (Postgres, SQL Server, InnoDB) LSM tree (Cassandra, RocksDB, LevelDB)
Writes In-place update; random I/O Append to memtable → flush sorted files → compact. Sequential
Write amplification Lower per write, but random Higher (compaction), but sequential
Reads Predictable, ~1 tree descent May check several SSTables (+ Bloom filters to skip)
Range scans Excellent (linked leaves) Good
Space Fragmentation Compaction reclaims; temporary 2× during compaction
Best for Read-heavy, mixed, transactional Write-heavy ingest

3. Indexing — the highest-ROI database skill

3.1 Index types

Type Structure Use
B-tree Balanced tree Default. Equality, range, ORDER BY, prefix LIKE 'abc%'
Hash Hash table Equality only, no ranges (Postgres)
Composite B-tree over multiple columns Multi-column predicates — column order is critical
Covering / INCLUDE Extra columns stored at the leaf Eliminates the lookup back to the table
Filtered / partial WHERE IsDeleted = 0 Small index over a hot subset; huge savings on soft-delete tables
Unique Enforces uniqueness Also a constraint — the DB is the only reliable place for this
Full-text / GIN Inverted index Text search, JSON containment, arrays
Spatial / GiST R-tree Geo queries
Columnstore Column-oriented, compressed Analytics/aggregation over millions of rows

3.2 The rules that matter

Rule 1 — Composite index column order: Equality, Range, Sort (the "ESR" rule).

-- Query
SELECT trade_id, notional FROM trades
WHERE portfolio_id = @p AND trade_date >= @from
ORDER BY trade_date DESC;

-- Correct index: equality column first, then the range/sort column
CREATE INDEX ix_trades_portfolio_date
    ON trades (portfolio_id, trade_date DESC)
    INCLUDE (notional);          -- covering: no lookup back to the table

(trade_date, portfolio_id) would be far worse: the engine can't seek directly to a portfolio, it must scan a date range and filter.

Rule 2 — Left-most prefix. An index on (A, B, C) serves WHERE A, WHERE A AND B, WHERE A AND B AND C. It does not efficiently serve WHERE B or WHERE C alone.

Rule 3 — Predicates must be SARGable (Search ARGument-able: the column appears bare on one side).

-- ❌ Non-SARGable: a function on the column defeats the index → full scan
WHERE YEAR(trade_date) = 2026
WHERE UPPER(client_name) = 'ACME'
WHERE notional * 1.2 > 1000
WHERE CAST(client_id AS varchar) = '42'      -- implicit conversion, a silent killer

-- ✔ SARGable equivalents
WHERE trade_date >= '2026-01-01' AND trade_date < '2027-01-01'
WHERE client_name = 'ACME'                    -- with a case-insensitive collation
WHERE notional > 1000 / 1.2
WHERE client_id = 42

⚠️ Implicit conversion is the most common invisible cause of a full scan: an nvarchar parameter compared to a varchar column, or EF Core sending nvarchar(4000) for a varchar(50) column. It shows in the plan as CONVERT_IMPLICIT. Fix by matching types in the mapping.

Rule 4 — Every index costs writes. Each INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must maintain every affected index. A table with 12 indexes has slow writes and a large footprint. Audit for unused indexes (sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats in SQL Server, pg_stat_user_indexes in Postgres) and drop them.

Rule 5 — Selectivity decides whether the index is used. An index on a column with 2 distinct values over 10M rows is useless for WHERE flag = 1 (the optimiser correctly chooses a scan — reading 50% of a table via an index is slower than scanning). It is useful as a filtered index or as the second column of a composite.

Rule 6 — Index the foreign keys. Missing FK indexes cause slow deletes on the parent (the DB must scan children to check the constraint) and slow joins. Most engines do not create these automatically (MySQL does; SQL Server and Postgres do not).

3.3 Reading an execution plan

Operator Meaning When it's a problem
Index Seek Direct tree descent ✔ What you want
Index Scan Read the whole index OK for small tables/analytics; bad on a large table with a selective predicate
Table/Clustered Index Scan Read every row Usually a missing or unusable index
Key/RID Lookup Seek in a nonclustered index, then fetch the row Fine occasionally; thousands of them ⇒ add INCLUDE columns
Nested Loops join For each outer row, seek inner Good when the outer is small; catastrophic when the estimate was wrong
Hash Match join Build a hash of one side Good for large unsorted sets; uses memory, may spill to disk
Merge join Both inputs sorted Very efficient when inputs are already ordered
Sort Explicit sort Expensive; can often be removed by an index in the right order
Spool Materialised intermediate Often a sign of a rewriteable query
Parallelism (Gather Streams) Multi-core execution Fine, unless you see excessive CXPACKET waits

The single most useful habit: compare estimated vs actual rows. A 1000× discrepancy means the optimiser was misled (stale statistics, parameter sniffing, non-SARGable predicate, table variable, a scalar UDF) and the plan choice is probably wrong.

-- SQL Server
SET STATISTICS IO, TIME ON;
-- then read "logical reads" per table: that's the real cost currency

-- Postgres
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT TEXT) SELECT ...;

⚠️ Parameter sniffing: the plan is compiled for the first parameter value and cached. A query optimised for @clientId = 'tiny-client' (nested loops) then runs for 'huge-client' and takes 40 minutes. Fixes: OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN, RECOMPILE, a local variable, or split into separate stored procedures. This is a classic senior-level SQL Server question.

4. Schema design

4.1 Normal forms — what they actually prevent

Form Rule Prevents
1NF Atomic values, no repeating groups Comma-separated lists in a column (unqueryable, unindexable)
2NF 1NF + no partial dependency on part of a composite key Redundancy tied to a key fragment
3NF 2NF + no transitive dependency (non-key → non-key) Update anomalies: changing a city's postcode in 10,000 rows
BCNF Every determinant is a candidate key Edge cases of 3NF

Practical guidance: normalise to 3NF, then denormalise deliberately with a documented reason. Each denormalisation is a promise to keep two copies in sync — and a bug waiting for the path you forgot.

Legitimate denormalisation: a computed order_total (updated in the same transaction as lines), a comment_count counter, a materialised view for a dashboard, a flattened reporting table. Illegitimate: "joins are slow" without measuring — a join on an indexed FK is not slow.

4.2 Data type discipline

Do Don't Why
decimal(19,4) for money float/real Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1; sums drift. Financial data in float is a defect
datetime2/timestamptz, store UTC datetime, local time Precision, DST, and timezone bugs
int/bigint sized to the actual range bigint for everything Storage × every index
varchar(n)/nvarchar(n) with a real n nvarchar(max) by default max columns are stored off-row and kill performance
bit/boolean char(1) with 'Y'/'N' Type safety
A proper enum/lookup table Magic ints Readability + referential integrity
uniqueidentifier only where needed GUID PKs everywhere See §2.1

Nullability: NOT NULL by default. Every nullable column is a question the reader must answer ("what does null mean here — unknown, not applicable, or not yet?"). And remember NULL breaks intuition: NULL = NULL is unknown, COUNT(col) skips nulls, NOT IN (subquery with a null) returns nothing.

4.3 Constraints are cheap correctness

ALTER TABLE trades ADD CONSTRAINT ck_trades_notional_positive CHECK (notional > 0);
ALTER TABLE trades ADD CONSTRAINT fk_trades_portfolio
    FOREIGN KEY (portfolio_id) REFERENCES portfolios(id);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_holdings_portfolio_instrument
    ON holdings (portfolio_id, instrument_id) WHERE is_deleted = 0;

Application-level validation is not a substitute. There will always be a second writer: a migration script, a support fix, an integration, a bug. The database is the last line of defence and the only one that sees every write.

4.4 Common patterns

Pattern Implementation Watch out
Soft delete is_deleted bit + filtered indexes + a global query filter Every query must filter; unique constraints must be filtered too
Audit trail Temporal tables (SQL Server), triggers, or an append-only history table Triggers are invisible — document them loudly
Optimistic concurrency rowversion/xmin column, WHERE version = @v, check rows affected EF Core [Timestamp] / IsRowVersion()
Hierarchies Adjacency list (parent_id) + recursive CTE; or materialised path; or closure table Adjacency is simplest; closure table for heavy read of ancestors
Multi-tenancy tenant_id on every table + RLS + query filters One missed filter = data breach (file 07 §9)
Slowly changing dimensions Type 2: valid_from/valid_to rows Query with BETWEEN; index on the key + valid_to
Enum storage tinyint + a lookup table with an FK Keeps the value readable in ad-hoc SQL

5. Transactions & isolation

5.1 ACID

  • Atomicity — all or nothing (via the log + rollback).
  • Consistency — constraints hold before and after (your job, plus the DB's constraints).
  • Isolation — concurrent transactions don't corrupt each other (via locks or MVCC).
  • Durability — committed means survivable (via WAL + fsync).

5.2 The anomalies and the isolation levels that prevent them

Anomaly What happens
Dirty read You read another transaction's uncommitted change; it rolls back
Non-repeatable read You read a row twice in one transaction and get different values
Phantom read You re-run a range query and new rows have appeared
Lost update Two transactions read-modify-write; one overwrites the other
Write skew Two transactions read overlapping data, write disjoint rows, and together violate an invariant (e.g. both doctors go off-call because each saw the other on-call)
Isolation level Dirty Non-repeatable Phantom Write skew Cost
Read Uncommitted ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ Lowest
Read Committed ✔ ✗ ✗ ✗ Default in SQL Server, Postgres, Oracle
Snapshot / RC-Snapshot (MVCC) ✔ ✔ ✔ ✗ Readers don't block writers
Repeatable Read ✔ ✔ ✗ (✔ in InnoDB) ✗ Higher
Serializable ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ Highest; may abort transactions

Locking vs MVCC:

  • Locking (SQL Server default READ COMMITTED): readers take shared locks → readers block writers and vice versa. This is why one long report can freeze an OLTP system.
  • MVCC (Postgres, Oracle, SQL Server with READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON): readers see a consistent snapshot; readers never block writers. Cost: version storage (Postgres bloat → autovacuum; SQL Server tempdb version store).

💡 Practical recommendation for SQL Server OLTP: turn on READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT. It eliminates the most common class of blocking with minimal behaviour change. Test first — it changes concurrency semantics for read-modify-write patterns.

⚠️ WITH (NOLOCK) is not a performance tuning tool. It is READ UNCOMMITTED: you can read uncommitted rows, read the same row twice, or miss rows entirely during a page split. It is acceptable only for approximate monitoring queries. Its ubiquity in enterprise codebases is a cargo cult.

5.3 Lost update — the bug you will actually hit

-- ❌ Two concurrent sessions both read 100, both write 90. Ten units vanish.
SELECT quantity FROM inventory WHERE id = 1;        -- app reads 100
-- ... app computes 100 - 10 ...
UPDATE inventory SET quantity = 90 WHERE id = 1;

-- ✔ Option A: atomic, let the DB do the arithmetic
UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - 10
WHERE id = 1 AND quantity >= 10;                    -- also enforces non-negative
-- check rows affected = 1

-- ✔ Option B: optimistic concurrency
UPDATE inventory SET quantity = @new, version = version + 1
WHERE id = 1 AND version = @readVersion;
-- rows affected = 0 → someone else won → reload and retry

-- ✔ Option C: pessimistic
SELECT quantity FROM inventory WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK) WHERE id = 1;  -- SQL Server
SELECT quantity FROM inventory WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;               -- Postgres/MySQL

5.4 Deadlocks

Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs. The engine detects the cycle and kills the cheaper victim.

T1: UPDATE accounts WHERE id=1   (holds lock on 1)
T2: UPDATE accounts WHERE id=2   (holds lock on 2)
T1: UPDATE accounts WHERE id=2   (waits for T2)
T2: UPDATE accounts WHERE id=1   (waits for T1)  → deadlock

Prevention:

  1. Always acquire locks in a consistent order (e.g. always ascending by primary key). This alone eliminates most deadlocks.
  2. Keep transactions short — never do I/O, HTTP calls, or wait for user input inside a transaction.
  3. Use the lowest sufficient isolation; enable snapshot isolation.
  4. Access tables in the same order across all code paths.
  5. Retry on deadlock (error 1205 in SQL Server, 40001 in Postgres) with backoff — deadlocks are expected under load, not exceptional.
// EF Core: retry on transient failures including deadlocks
services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(o => o.UseSqlServer(cs, sql =>
    sql.EnableRetryOnFailure(maxRetryCount: 3,
                             maxRetryDelay: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5),
                             errorNumbersToAdd: [1205])));

⚠️ With EnableRetryOnFailure, user-initiated transactions must be wrapped in an execution strategy or EF throws — a common gotcha.

5.5 Long transactions are poison

A transaction open for 30 seconds holds locks and (in MVCC systems) prevents version cleanup for everyone. Pattern to avoid: BEGIN TRAN → call an external API → COMMIT. Do the I/O outside; use the outbox pattern if the write and the call must both happen.

6. Writing efficient SQL

6.1 The recurring problems

Problem Symptom Fix
N+1 queries 1 query for the list + 1 per row Join, IN, or EF Include/split query. The single most common ORM performance bug
SELECT * Extra I/O, breaks covering indexes, breaks on schema change Name the columns
Missing pagination Loads 500k rows into memory Keyset pagination (below)
Function on an indexed column Full scan SARGable rewrite (§3.2)
Implicit conversion Full scan Match parameter types
OR across different columns Often a scan UNION ALL of two seekable queries
Correlated subquery per row O(n) subqueries Rewrite as a join or window function
Scalar UDF in a WHERE/SELECT Row-by-row execution, no parallelism Inline it, or use an inline TVF
DISTINCT masking a bad join Duplicate rows from a fan-out join Fix the join
COUNT(*) on a huge table for paging Full scan every page Approximate count, or don't show a total

6.2 Pagination: OFFSET vs keyset

-- ❌ OFFSET degrades linearly: page 10,000 must read and discard 200,000 rows
SELECT * FROM trades ORDER BY trade_date DESC, id DESC
OFFSET 200000 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY;

-- ✔ Keyset ("seek") pagination: constant cost at any depth
SELECT TOP 20 * FROM trades
WHERE (trade_date, id) < (@lastDate, @lastId)      -- tuple comparison; index-supported
ORDER BY trade_date DESC, id DESC;

Keyset pagination requires a stable, unique sort key (add the PK as a tiebreaker) and can't jump to an arbitrary page number — which is almost always fine, because nobody clicks "page 4,271".

6.3 Window functions — replace self-joins and cursors

-- Latest holding per portfolio, without a correlated subquery
SELECT portfolio_id, instrument_id, weight, as_of
FROM (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY portfolio_id, instrument_id
                              ORDER BY as_of DESC) AS rn
    FROM holdings
) ranked
WHERE rn = 1;

-- Running total and period-over-period change in one pass
SELECT trade_date, notional,
       SUM(notional) OVER (ORDER BY trade_date
                           ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total,
       notional - LAG(notional) OVER (ORDER BY trade_date) AS day_change
FROM daily_flows;

6.4 Set-based, never row-by-row

-- ❌ RBAR (row by agonising row): a cursor doing 100k single-row updates
-- ✔ One statement
UPDATE h
SET    h.weight = h.market_value / p.total_value
FROM   holdings h
JOIN   portfolios p ON p.id = h.portfolio_id
WHERE  p.as_of = @asOf;

For very large updates, batch to avoid lock escalation and log growth:

WHILE 1 = 1
BEGIN
    UPDATE TOP (5000) holdings SET is_archived = 1
    WHERE is_archived = 0 AND as_of < @cutoff;
    IF @@ROWCOUNT = 0 BREAK;
    WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:00.100';       -- let other work through
END

6.5 Bulk loading

SqlBulkCopy (.NET), COPY (Postgres), LOAD DATA INFILE (MySQL), or table-valued parameters. Orders of magnitude faster than row inserts. For huge loads: drop non-clustered indexes, load, rebuild.

7. ORMs: EF Core specifics

Concern Guidance
Tracking AsNoTracking() for every read-only query — avoids building the change-tracker graph. Measurable on large result sets
Projection Select into a DTO. Never return entities from an API; you fetch columns you don't need and risk lazy-loading in the serialiser
N+1 Include/ThenInclude, or AsSplitQuery() when a single query produces a cartesian explosion
Lazy loading Off. It is the mechanism by which N+1 becomes invisible
Client evaluation EF Core throws instead of silently evaluating in memory (since 3.0) — good. If you see AsEnumerable() before a Where, that's a full table load
Raw SQL FromSqlInterpolated/SqlQuery<T> — parameterised automatically. Use it for complex reporting queries; don't fight LINQ
Bulk operations ExecuteUpdateAsync/ExecuteDeleteAsync (EF7+) generate a single statement — no loading entities
Compiled queries EF.CompileAsyncQuery for hot paths (saves expression-tree translation)
Migrations Review the generated SQL every time. Auto-generated migrations happily write a table-rebuild that locks production
Concurrency IsRowVersion() + handle DbUpdateConcurrencyException
Pooling AddDbContextPool for high-throughput APIs 
// A read query shaped correctly
var rows = await db.Trades
    .AsNoTracking()
    .Where(t => t.PortfolioId == portfolioId && t.TradeDate >= from)
    .OrderByDescending(t => t.TradeDate)
    .Select(t => new TradeListItem(t.Id, t.InstrumentCode, t.Notional, t.TradeDate))  // projection
    .Take(200)
    .ToListAsync(ct);

🧪 Always log the generated SQL in development (EnableSensitiveDataLogging in dev only) and read it. The gap between what you think LINQ does and what it emits is where the performance goes.

When to drop to Dapper/raw SQL: complex reporting, window functions, bulk operations, recursive CTEs, or any query where you want to control the plan. Mixing EF Core (writes, domain) + Dapper (reads) is a mainstream, defensible architecture — that's CQRS level 2 (file 07 §6).

8. Scaling relational databases

flowchart LR
    A[Slow] --> B[Index + query tuning]
    B --> C[Cache reads]
    C --> D[Vertical scale]
    D --> E[Read replicas]
    E --> F[Partition tables]
    F --> G[Shard / split by bounded context]
    G --> H[Different store for the hot workload]

8.1 Connection pooling

Connections are expensive (auth, TLS, session state). Pool them — ADO.NET does by default (Max Pool Size=100). ⚠️ Pool exhaustion presents as Timeout expired. The timeout period elapsed prior to obtaining a connection from the pool and is nearly always caused by leaked connections (missing using) or long-running queries holding connections. Sizing rule of thumb: pool size ≈ cores × 2 + effective_spindles per app instance — more connections than the DB can run concurrently just adds queueing. For serverless/many-instance topologies, use an external pooler (PgBouncer).

8.2 Partitioning (within one database)

Split one logical table into physical partitions by a key (usually date). Benefits: partition elimination (queries touch only relevant partitions), fast archival (SWITCH/DETACH a partition instead of deleting millions of rows), per-partition maintenance. Requirements: the partition key must be in the query predicate, and it must be part of every unique index. Not a substitute for indexing.

8.3 Read replicas

Offload reporting and read-heavy endpoints. ⚠️ Replication lag → stale reads (file 08 §4.3). Route explicitly:

// Separate connection strings/DbContexts for read vs write is clearer than a magic router
services.AddDbContext<WriteDbContext>(o => o.UseSqlServer(primaryCs));
services.AddDbContext<ReadDbContext>(o  => o.UseSqlServer(replicaCs)
    .UseQueryTrackingBehavior(QueryTrackingBehavior.NoTracking));

8.4 High availability

Mechanism RPO RTO Notes
Backups + PITR Minutes (log backup interval) Hours Mandatory baseline. Test restores
Log shipping Minutes Minutes–hours Cheap DR
Always On AG / Postgres streaming replication ~0 (sync) or seconds (async) Seconds–minutes Standard HA
Managed multi-AZ (Azure SQL, RDS) Seconds ~1 min Least operational work
Active-active multi-region — — Conflict resolution required; rarely worth it for OLTP

Backup rule: 3-2-1 (three copies, two media, one offsite), plus a scheduled restore drill. An untested backup is a hypothesis.

9. Migrations & schema evolution

Expand → migrate → contract (file 02 §5.2) applied to schemas:

Change Safe approach
Add a column Nullable or with a default (⚠️ in older engines, a non-null default rewrites the whole table — check your version)
Rename a column Add new → dual-write → backfill → switch reads → drop old. Never a direct rename — it breaks running instances mid-deploy
Drop a column Stop writing → stop reading → wait a release → drop
Change a type New column + backfill + switch (same as rename)
Add an index CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (Postgres) / ONLINE = ON (SQL Server Enterprise); otherwise expect a lock
Add NOT NULL Add nullable → backfill in batches → add the constraint with NOT VALID then VALIDATE (Postgres)
Add a foreign key Add NOT VALID, validate separately, to avoid a long table lock

Rules: migrations are versioned, forward-only in production, reviewed as SQL, tested against a production-sized copy, and never edited after being applied anywhere. Long-running data backfills belong in a batched background job, not in a migration that blocks the deployment.

10. Observability & troubleshooting

What to monitor: p95/p99 query duration, active connections vs pool size, blocked/waiting sessions, deadlocks/min, buffer cache hit ratio, page life expectancy (SQL Server), replication lag, disk latency (avg_disk_sec/read — should be < 10 ms, < 1 ms on good SSD), log growth, index fragmentation, and top queries by total CPU and total logical reads (not by single-execution duration — a 10 ms query run 1M times is the real cost).

-- SQL Server: the 10 most expensive queries by total CPU
SELECT TOP 10
    qs.total_worker_time / 1000 AS total_cpu_ms,
    qs.execution_count,
    qs.total_worker_time / qs.execution_count / 1000 AS avg_cpu_ms,
    qs.total_logical_reads / qs.execution_count AS avg_reads,
    SUBSTRING(st.text, (qs.statement_start_offset/2) + 1,
        ((CASE qs.statement_end_offset WHEN -1 THEN DATALENGTH(st.text)
          ELSE qs.statement_end_offset END - qs.statement_start_offset)/2) + 1) AS statement_text
FROM sys.dm_exec_query_stats qs
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(qs.sql_handle) st
ORDER BY qs.total_worker_time DESC;

-- Who is blocking whom, right now
SELECT r.session_id, r.blocking_session_id, r.wait_type, r.wait_time,
       r.status, t.text
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests r
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) t
WHERE r.blocking_session_id <> 0;

-- Postgres: extension pg_stat_statements is the equivalent
SELECT calls, mean_exec_time, total_exec_time, query
FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10;

-- Bloat / vacuum health
SELECT relname, n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC;

A tuning method that works:

  1. Find the top query by total cost (not the slowest single run).
  2. Read its plan; find the operator consuming the most rows/reads.
  3. Check estimated vs actual rows.
  4. Fix the cause: index, rewrite, statistics, or schema.
  5. Measure again. Then check that you didn't slow down writes.

11. Security (see also file 13)

  • Parameterised queries only. No string concatenation, ever, including in dynamic SQL (use sp_executesql with parameters).
  • Least privilege: the application login should not be db_owner. Separate read-only and read-write logins where practical.
  • Encryption: TLS in transit; TDE at rest; column-level encryption or Always Encrypted for the most sensitive fields.
  • Row-level security for multi-tenant defence in depth.
  • Auditing on sensitive tables; log who accessed PII, not just what changed.
  • No production data in dev. Mask or synthesise. GDPR applies to your test database too.
  • Secrets: managed identity / integrated auth over passwords in connection strings.

12. Checklist & interview angles

Schema/query review checklist

  • PK narrow, unique, static, ever-increasing
  • FKs indexed
  • Constraints (NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE, FK) express the real rules
  • Money as decimal, timestamps as UTC with timezone-aware types
  • Indexes match the actual query predicates (ESR order); no unused indexes
  • All predicates SARGable; no implicit conversions
  • No SELECT *, no unbounded result sets, keyset pagination for deep pages
  • Transactions short; no I/O inside; consistent lock ordering; retry on deadlock
  • Isolation level chosen deliberately; snapshot isolation considered
  • N+1 checked by reading the emitted SQL
  • Migration is expand/contract-safe and tested at production data volume
  • Backup + tested restore; RPO/RTO documented

🔍 Interview angles

  • Clustered vs nonclustered index? Clustered defines physical row order (the table is the index); nonclustered is a separate structure pointing back via the clustering key.
  • Why did adding an index make writes slower? Every DML must maintain it; plus page splits and more log volume.
  • What's a covering index? One that contains every column the query needs (key + INCLUDE), so no lookup to the base table.
  • Explain isolation levels and pick one for a banking transfer. Serializable or explicit locking for the balance check + debit; or an atomic conditional UPDATE with a CHECK constraint — the latter is usually better.
  • How do you find and fix a slow query? Top-by-total-cost → plan → estimated vs actual rows → index/rewrite/statistics → re-measure.
  • SQL vs NoSQL for this? Answer by access pattern and consistency needs, not by scale folklore (file 11 §1).
  • How do you delete 100M rows without downtime? Batched deletes with a delay, or partition switch, or create-new-table-and-swap.
  • What breaks first when the table hits a billion rows? Not seeks — scans, COUNT(*), unpartitioned maintenance, and index rebuild windows.
